body_markdown:
What eventually became the 1960–69 Mercury Comet had a somewhat interesting and complicated gestation. Initially, it was supposed to be a compact companion to the Edsel line, but due to the brand’s unceremonious axing, the car became just plain Comet for 1960. (Apparently, the[perpetually frowning Robert McNamara helped push Edsel off the cliff](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/the-man-who-killed-the-edsel-even-before-it-failed/) before it even really got going.)


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Yes, that’s right. In 1960 (and again in ’61), it was simply the Comet, with no Mercury badging to be seen anywhere. Of course, the vehicle was sold in Lincoln-Mercury dealerships, so most people likely thought of it as a Mercury. And L-M division itself would officially make it a Mercury[in 1962](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/mercury/comet/1962) .


Thomas Klockau


Early Comets were easily discernible from their Falcon siblings from the back by their fins and “cat’s eye” taillights, and from the front by their quad headlights and broader chrome grille. Comets got a longer wheelbase too when compared to the Ford Falcon.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


From 1960 to 1963, its same basic overall look remained, though of course chrome trim, grilles, and other such things changed year to year. But then in 1964, though riding the same basic chassis and being much the same as the ’60–63 under the skin, Comets (and Falcons too)[got an all-new look.](http://lov2xlr8.no/brochures/mercury/64mco/bilder/1.jpg)


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


The overall look was more imposing. Gone were the fins, replaced by squared-off rear quarter panels. The two-door hardtops were especially attractive. Regardless of body style, all Comets got a rather Lincoln Continental–inspired grille. As expected, the usual coupe, sedan, wagon, and convertible body styles were offered, in trims from plain to pretty plush.[And of course, the top-of-the-line Comet station wagon, the Villager, had faux wood trim on the exterior.](http://lov2xlr8.no/brochures/mercury/64mco/bilder/9.jpg)


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


For 1965, the most noticeable new styling feature was up front, where stacked quad headlamps flanked a rather delicate-looking but attractive horizontal bar grille. As usual, the Villager, at $2703, was the fanciest and most expensive Comet station wagon.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


But it was *most definitely not* a sales sensation. Only 1592 Villager wagons, with a curb weight of 2500 pounds, were built in 1965. Even the non-woody Comet 404 wagon, at $2523, sold only 5226 examples.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


And the Comet 404 wagon was the most popular one that year,[as the cheapest Comet wagon, the 202](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/mercury/comet/1965/1965-mercury-comet-202?id=aCn1I000000CwA8SAK) , sold 4814 copies, despite its cheaper $2438 MSRP. I guess no one really was excited about small wagons that year, because Ford sold a total of 177,664 full-size wagons that same year.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


The Villager model added the simulated wood trim on the sides and tailgate—emulating Mercury’s biggest top-line wagon, the Colony Park—and also had a power rear window as standard. Wagons were 191.8 inches long, with a 109.5-inch wheelbase.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Today’s featured car was seen at the excellent[Trains, Planes + Automobiles](https://geneseo.org/tpa) show held every Labor Day weekend in downtown Geneseo, Illinois. I saw this car at two different times, in 2013 and again in 2016. I have not seen it since, so I think it may have been sold and moved away. The wood trim contrasted nicely with the Onyx paint.


Thomas Klockau


According to the info sheet on the dash, this car had the optional 289-cubic-inch V-8. Options included power steering ($86.30), power brakes, AM/FM radio ($129.30), exterior adjustable sideview mirror, day/night inside rearview mirror, and wire wheel covers ($64.40).


Thomas Klockau


Other Comet options that year included air conditioning ($257.50), tinted glass ($27.80), courtesy light group ($14.80), and padded dash ($18.40). A roof rack for wagons was $64.35.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


In addition to Onyx, other available Comet colors included Polar White, Blue Ice, Burgundy, Olive Mist, Tiffany Blue, Pecan Frost, Aquamarine and Carnival Red.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Literature described it as “…strong new, sleek new, all new edition of the world’s 100,000-mile durability champion! Last year a team of specially equipped Comets each went 100,000 miles at Daytona in 40 days and nights of continuous driving. This year’s Comet stands out again! Comet engines are bigger and more powerful!


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


“Comet for 1965 has a fresh, clean, classic look…a wider, lower, longer look accented by tasteful trim! New on the inside too, with luxurious interiors.”


For all that gushing prose, however, ’65 would be the last year for the original compact Comet. In 1966 an all-new, now midsize Comet would appear—a convertible version would even pace the Indy 500 that year—but it still bore a family resemblance to the ’65s, as the vertical quad headlamps continued. But that’s a story for another time!


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)
